Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 37

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Rumination: Revenge: ruminate about how to get even with assailant, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore, Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.

Vignette:
Samir stood at the edge of the lower valley when the river finally broke through. The water did not creep; it struck. He remembers the roar first, then the concrete groaning, then the sudden, violent tug of the current. He fought his way to the roof, but the sequence of what happened next fractured. One moment he was hauling his wife’s photo album to higher ground, the next he was clinging to an awning, screaming for help that never came. He cannot place the moments in order anymore. Some days he swears he sees his boots slip; other days he is certain he was already pulling himself over the parapet. When the memories surface, they arrive as a complete sensory assault. He hears the specific crack of the drainage pipe, feels the icy water soaking through his shirt, tastes the silt, and sees the gray sky pressing down. It does not feel like a memory. It feels like he is back there, drowning all over again. Samir had come to believe that safety was an illusion until it was mapped out. He started checking exits the moment he stepped into any room. At his office, a glass-walled tech hub downtown, he timed his walks to the stairwell, noting exactly how many paces from his desk it took to reach the lobby doors. He needed to know the perimeter. When a colleague dropped a pen behind him, Samir jerked his shoulders forward, heart hammering as if the current were pulling at his ankles again. He reacted with the same alarm when anyone approached from his blind spot. What frightened him most was the sheer unpredictability of a world that could turn violent without warning. He forced himself to tell the building he was fine, that the flood had been an anomaly, that he was stronger now. But when the quiet thoughts crept in, they twisted into a relentless cycle. He replayed the night on a loop, fixated on a specific figure who had stood in the doorway earlier, watching the water rise without offering a hand. Samir ruminated about how to get even with the assailant who had let him face it alone. To keep from being reminded of his vulnerability, he stopped going to clinics. When his wrist began to throb from a repetitive strain, he wrapped it in tape instead of scheduling an exam. Ambulances wailing outside made him pull the blinds shut, his breath catching as the siren’s pitch mimicked the sirens that had preceded the flood. At forty, his job as a software engineer demanded constant collaboration, but the open floor plan became a minefield. He sat facing the wall, writing code while his eyes tracked the main corridor. During stand-up meetings, he stood near the fire exit, his body coiled. When a project manager tapped his shoulder to hand over a keyboard, Samir flinched, dropping his hands to his sides until his pulse settled. He told his wife, Leila, that he was fine, but he had come to believe nothing good could happen to him anymore. He used to be a happy person, someone who could laugh at work or take a weekend drive without bracing for disaster. Now he was always miserable, convinced that his own poor judgment had placed him in the path of the water. Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation; he was certain he had deserved the current that dragged him under. The routine finally cracked during a quarterly product demo. A sudden power flicker made the overhead lights drop, and Samir was on his feet, scanning for exits, unable to speak as the room blurred around him. That night, he found himself staring at the ceiling, replaying the flood’s roar in his head, his mind drifting again to the face of the man who had watched him suffer. He realized he had stopped going to the gym, avoided the emergency room when Leila’s fever spiked, and flinched every time she reached for his arm across the dinner table. He was exhausted from mapping exits and forcing himself to think only positive thoughts, but the misery did not lift. He called a clinic. He doubted recovery was possible, but the weight of the water, the noise, and the constant vigilance had become too heavy to carry alone.
